back2basics.text: India regulates drugs through the Drugs and Cosmetics Act and Rules, which include the New Drugs and Clinical Trials Rules, 2019, and the Drugs Rules, 1945. The Central Licensing Authority grants permissions for manufacturing new drugs, while State Licensing Authorities issue manufacturing licenses. Bulk drugs are active or inactive substances used in formulations. Regulatory oversight ensures drug quality, safety, and efficacy to protect public health and prevent issues like antimicrobial resistance.

2026-11-20-pm-2f339b3201.deck: The Union Health Ministry has proposed amendments to the New Drugs and Clinical Trials Rules, 2019, and the Drugs Rules, 1945, to strengthen regulatory oversight of antimicrobials and introduce separate licensing for bulk drug wholesale. These changes aim to address antimicrobial resistance and improve accountability in pharmaceutical supply chains, important for public health governance.

structure.intro: The Union Health Ministry has proposed amendments to strengthen regulation of antimicrobials and bulk drug wholesale.

mcq.stem:
Consider the following statements about the recent amendments proposed by the Union Health Ministry:
1. Antimicrobials are proposed to be included under the definition of 'New Drug' requiring central approval before state licensing.
2. A common licence will continue to cover wholesale sale of both formulations and bulk drugs without distinction.
mcq.trap: Statement 2 is incorrect because the amendment proposes separate licensing forms for bulk drugs, distinct from formulations, replacing the common licence.

body.label: Inclusion in new drug definition
body.text: The amendment proposes to include 'antimicrobials' within the definition of 'New Drug' under Rule 2(1)(w)(v) to bring them under the regulatory framework of new drugs.

body.label: Central Licensing Authority role
body.text: Manufacturers of antimicrobials would need to obtain permission from the Central Licensing Authority before applying for a manufacturing licence from the State Licensing Authority.

body.label: Addressing antimicrobial resistance
body.text: This change aims to ensure quality, safety, and efficacy of antimicrobials by requiring studies like bioavailability, bioequivalence, and stability, thereby helping to combat antimicrobial resistance.

sections.heading: What changes are proposed for antimicrobials under the New Drugs and Clinical Trials Rules, 2019?

body.label: Separate licence forms introduced
body.text: The Drugs Rules, 1945, will be amended to introduce a separate application form (Form 19-BC) and licence form (Form 20-BC) specifically for wholesale sale of bulk drugs, distinct from formulations.

body.label: Focused regulatory oversight
body.text: This dedicated licensing framework will enable better control and accountability in the wholesale distribution of bulk drugs, including those under the Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act.

body.label: Supervision and compliance
body.text: Wholesale sale of bulk drugs will be carried out under the personal supervision of a competent person to strengthen accountability in distribution and handling.

body.label: Transition period for existing licensees
body.text: Existing licensees will have time to comply, with new requirements applying after their current retention period expires or 12 months after final amendment publication, whichever is later.

sections.heading: How will the licensing framework for bulk drug wholesale be modified?

body.label: Regulatory flexibility for certain drugs
body.text: Amendments to the Drugs Rules, 1945, propose regulatory flexibility under revised Schedule M for medicinal gases, empty gelatin capsules, and disinfectant fluids.

body.label: Exemptions continuation
body.text: The Drugs Technical Advisory Board recommended continuing exemptions available under the pre-revised Schedule M for these categories, as some revised provisions are not relevant to their manufacturing.

body.label: Maintaining quality standards
body.text: The amendments aim to align regulatory requirements with manufacturing processes without diluting quality, safety, or oversight standards.

sections.heading: What other regulatory amendments are proposed for specific drug categories?

back2basics.text: Government securities are debt instruments issued by the government to borrow money from the public. Underwriting auctions involve primary dealers committing to buy a minimum amount of securities to ensure full subscription, helping the government raise funds efficiently. The Reserve Bank of India conducts these auctions electronically, setting commission rates for primary dealers who facilitate the sale. These securities also play a role in banks' liquidity management and regulatory requirements.

2026-11-20-pm-4c25c5ba39.deck: The Reserve Bank of India conducted an underwriting auction for Government Securities worth ₹33,000 crore on November 20, 2026. This auction is crucial for understanding government borrowing, the role of primary dealers, and RBI's monetary policy operations.

body: RBI organizes underwriting and competitive auctions involving primary dealers to ensure full subscription of government debt.
The auction process sets interest rates on government securities, influencing borrowing costs and market liquidity.
Government securities form part of banks' Statutory Liquidity Ratio, affecting credit availability and monetary policy transmission.
structure.conclusion: Thus, RBI's auction mechanism is a key tool for managing government finances and monetary policy.
structure.intro: RBI conducts auctions of government securities to facilitate government borrowing and manage liquidity.

mcq.stem:
Consider the following statements about the RBI underwriting auction conducted on November 20, 2026:
1. The auction involved Government Securities worth ₹33,000 crore including 6.53% GS 2031 and 7.71% GS 2066.
2. The underwriting commission cut-off rate was higher for 6.53% GS 2031 than for 7.71% GS 2066.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
mcq.trap: Statement 2 is incorrect because the underwriting commission cut-off rate was 0.39 paise per ₹100 for 6.53% GS 2031, which is lower than 0.78 paise per ₹100 for 7.71% GS 2066.

body.label: Auction details
body.text: RBI conducted an underwriting auction for the sale of Government Securities worth ₹33,000 crore, comprising two securities: 6.53% GS 2031 (₹19,000 crore) and 7.71% GS 2066 (₹14,000 crore).

body.label: Primary Dealers' role
body.text: Primary Dealers (PDs) were required to meet Minimum Underwriting Commitment (MUC) and could participate in Additional Competitive Underwriting (ACU) auctions, bidding electronically via RBI's e-Kuber system.

body.label: Auction method and timing
body.text: The auction used a multiple price-based method and was held between 9:00 A.M. and 9:30 A.M. on November 20, 2026.

sections.heading: What was the underwriting auction conducted by RBI on November 20, 2026?

body.label: Auction outcome
body.text: The total amount underwritten matched the notified amount of ₹33,000 crore, with ₹19,000 crore for 6.53% GS 2031 and ₹14,000 crore for 7.71% GS 2066.

body.label: Commission rates
body.text: RBI set the cut-off underwriting commission rates payable to Primary Dealers at 0.39 paise per ₹100 for 6.53% GS 2031 and 0.78 paise per ₹100 for 7.71% GS 2066.

body.label: Monetary policy impact
body.text: Such auctions help RBI manage government borrowing requirements and influence liquidity in the financial system.

sections.heading: What were the results and significance of the underwriting auction?

body.label: State securities auction
body.text: Separate auctions for State Government Securities amounting to ₹31,950 crore were scheduled for November 23, 2026, involving multiple states and various tenors.

body.label: Bidding process
body.text: Both competitive and non-competitive bids are accepted electronically via RBI's e-Kuber system, with non-competitive bids also accepted through the Retail Direct portal.

body.label: Investment and regulatory aspects
body.text: State Government Securities qualify as eligible investments for banks under the Statutory Liquidity Ratio and are governed by the Government Securities Act, 2006.

back2basics.text: A trilateral summit is a formal meeting involving the leaders of three countries to discuss issues of mutual interest, often related to diplomacy, security, and economic cooperation. Such summits are significant as they can shape international relations and influence global power structures.
